No source mentions any vegetarian or vegan broth/noodle option — fish- and meat-derived stock is central to essentially every dish, so vegan and vegetarian diners should treat this shop as unsuitable.

One aggregator reported a different, possibly older schedule: weekdays 11:00-15:45 and 17:00-21:00 (split), weekends/holidays 11:00-21:00 straight through. Confirm current hours before visiting.

chef_bio.background: The Asakusa branch opened on August 16, 2018, under the sign "中華そば専門 田中そば店" (Chūka-soba Specialist Tanaka Sobaten). It took over the storefront that had previously housed an Aomori-style niboshi ramen shop called "つし馬" (Tsushima). The parent company, Tanaka Shoten, opened its first shop in Adachi-ku in December 2000 and gradually expanded across Tokyo and beyond (Asakusa, Sendai, Akihabara, Misato — a 15th location opened in February 2021), always chasing the same simple goal: 'oishii' (delicious).
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's guiding idea is 気軽に食べる田舎そば — 'unpretentious, countryside-style soba you can eat without fuss' — aiming for a nostalgic, almost salt-ramen-like flavor built on a niboshi-and-shoyu broth.
chef_bio.specialty: Chūka soba (a niboshi/dried-sardine and shoyu based broth reminiscent of Kitakata-style ramen) and the Asakusa-exclusive Tsugaru Niboshi Ramen and Bari Niboshi Soba, which revive dishes from the shop's Tsushima-era predecessor.

anecdotes.text: The Asakusa shop occupies the former location of the Aomori niboshi ramen shop Tsushima, and keeps two of that shop's dishes alive as an Asakusa-only menu: Tsugaru Niboshi Ramen and Bari Niboshi Soba.
Tanaka Shoten's company history traces from its December 2000 opening in Adachi-ku through expansion into Asakusa, Sendai, Akihabara and Misato, guided by a consistent focus on 'oishii'.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering goes through a ticket vending machine (券売機) at the entrance with no table service to guide you, so being able to point at pictures/buttons and pay cash is enough — a little comfort with a Japanese-only setup helps, but no conversation is required.

tokyo_marugoto_hokkaido_asakus.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu, labeling, or allergy protocol was found in any source. The all-you-can-eat courses include tempura-battered crab and other fried items, crab hot pot with shared broth, and likely soy-sauce-based seasonings — a high-risk setting for a strict gluten-free or celiac diet, with no evidence the kitchen accommodates it.
tokyo_marugoto_hokkaido_asakus.vegan_detail: This is a crab and Hokkaido seafood specialty restaurant centered on all-you-can-eat crab courses, crab hot pot, and kani-zōsui; no plant-based, vegetarian, or vegan menu items were found in any source, and the food concept (crab sashimi, hot pot, tempura, congee) is seafood-based throughout with no indication of dashi alternatives.

chef_bio.origin: Asakusa, Tokyo — sister restaurant to the company's Jingisukan tavern and Hokkaido product shop nearby
chef_bio.background: Marugoto Hokkaido ("All of Hokkaido") started as an Asakusa antenna shop bringing Hokkaido specialty foods to Tokyo, and this Asakusa branch built an izakaya around that sourcing model: king crab (tarabagani), snow crab (zuwaigani) and hair crab (kegani) shipped in directly from Hokkaido and served in all-you-can-eat courses just off Kokusai-dori, a one-minute walk from Tsukuba Express Asakusa Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: A Hokkaido antenna-shop concept — deliver Hokkaido's crab and seafood directly to Asakusa at approachable prices rather than treating crab as a rare luxury.
chef_bio.specialty: Three-crab all-you-can-eat course (king crab, snow crab, hair crab) served as sashimi, crab hot pot, grilled and fried crab, and finished with kani-zōsui (crab rice porridge); the restaurant recommends its house-made crab vinegar (自家製カニ酢) as a condiment for the crab.

anecdotes.text: A local Taito-ward feature piece calls crab "the king of winter flavors" and highlights being able to eat one's fill of it casually at this Asakusa shop.

cultural_comfort.note: No confirmed English menu or English-speaking-staff information was found, so expect a Japanese-language, locals-and-tour-group izakaya experience despite the Asakusa tourist-district location.

tokyo_ginkado.gf_detail: Daifuku mochi and red bean (anko) filling are naturally wheat-free by nature, but the shop has not published anything about the dusting starch used (potato starch vs. wheat flour), shared prep surfaces, or cross-contact with the custard/cream-based daifuku flavors. No dedicated gluten-free process has been confirmed — ask staff directly before eating if you have celiac disease.

The strawberry skewers (ichigo-kushi) are fresh fruit, typically with a sugar glaze. None of this has been explicitly confirmed as vegan by the shop itself, so ask staff before ordering.

chef_bio.background: Originally a kanzashi (hair ornament) and Japanese craft-goods shop founded roughly 280 years ago near Sensoji Temple on Nakamise-dori — the shop name "Ginka" (銀花, "silver flower") is said to derive from the ornamental kanzashi it sold to geisha. After foot traffic collapsed during the COVID-19 pandemic, the shop was renewed in 2022 from a traditional crafts store into a fruit-and-wagashi sweets stall.
chef_bio.specialty: Ichigo daifuku (strawberry mochi with red bean paste) and ichigo-kushi (fresh strawberry skewers)

anecdotes.text: The shop began as a kanzashi outfitter near Sensoji roughly 280 years ago; its name references the ornamental "silver flowers" (kanzashi) it originally sold.

The old crafts shop was reborn in 2022 as a fruit and wagashi sweets stand after pandemic-era foot traffic on Nakamise-dori dried up; it now sells strawberry skewers, cut melon, and strawberry daifuku.
A visiting blogger described the strawberry daifuku as filled with a plump, juicy strawberry paired with gently sweetened red bean paste and soft mochi.

cultural_comfort.note: A walk-up sweets stand on Tokyo's most tourist-trodden street — you can order by pointing at the photo menu, but there's no confirmed English signage or English-speaking staff, so a little Japanese or gestures help, especially for allergy questions.

tokyo_suzuyoshi.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu, labeling, or accommodation is documented anywhere. The menu is built around grilled skewers with tare glaze, miso-based motsu-ni, and a soy-based Korean-style beef tendon stew — tare and miso in Japanese izakaya cooking are almost always wheat-containing (soy sauce), and there is no mention of a dedicated fryer or wheat-free soy sauce option. Treat as unsafe for celiac diners.
tokyo_suzuyoshi.vegan_detail: The entire menu is meat/offal/seafood-centered (yakitori, motsu-ni, beef tendon stew, whelk, sashimi, grilled fish); no plant-based or vegetarian dishes were identified in any source, and dashi/stock use is unconfirmed but presumed to be conventional (likely katsuo/bonito-based). Not suitable for vegan diners.

chef_bio.origin: Asakusa (opened 1974)
chef_bio.background: Suzuyoshi has stood on Asakusa's Hoppy-dori since 1974 and is regularly cited as one of the street's most historic surviving taverns — a holdout of the postwar Showa-era drinking-street atmosphere as many neighboring bars have closed or been rebuilt amid the area's redevelopment around the Tokyo Skytree and the Olympics. A visiting food writer who first came roughly twenty years ago recalled the building still had an external staircase up to a residential unit above the bar, a detail that has since disappeared as the block modernized.
chef_bio.specialty: Draft (nama/taru-nama) Hoppy — Suzuyoshi is widely cited as the only shop left on Hoppy-dori that still pours genuine draft Hoppy rather than the bottled version, served white, black, or half-and-half. It's paired with a spicy, Korean-influenced beef tendon stew (piri-kara gyusuji-ni) and a miso-based motsu-ni (offal stew), alongside grilled skewers, whelk simmered in soy, sashimi, and grilled fish.

anecdotes.text: 浅草ホッピー通りでも屈指の歴史を誇る『鈴芳』は、このお店でしか飲めないという樽生ホッピーやピリ辛テイストの韓国風牛すじ煮が人気です。

The author recalls a visit roughly 20 years earlier when the building still had an outdoor staircase leading to an upstairs residence — a vestige of Showa-era Hoppy-dori that has largely vanished as the surrounding blocks were rebuilt.

cultural_comfort.note: Cash-only, walk-in-only Shitamachi tavern with no confirmed English menu; one visitor account describes being brushed off when asking for an English menu, so English-speaking first-timers will likely be more comfortable with a translation app or local companion.

tokyo_nitenmon_yabu.gf_detail: No gluten-free options, dedicated fryer, or gluten-free preparation were mentioned in any available source. As a conventional soba shop, the noodles are very likely a standard wheat-blended (tsunagi) soba rather than 100% buckwheat (jūwari), and the dipping sauce (tsuyu) and other dishes would be expected to use ordinary wheat-based soy sauce and bonito dashi — but this restaurant-specific detail was not directly confirmed in sourced material. Celiac or strictly gluten-free diners should not consider this a safe option without calling ahead.
tokyo_nitenmon_yabu.vegan_detail: No vegan menu, plant-based options, or accommodations were mentioned in any available source. The shop's signature dish is a pork cutlet rice bowl (katsudon), and as a conventional soba/udon shop its broths and tsuyu almost certainly rely on standard bonito (katsuo) dashi throughout the menu. No confirmation of a kombu-only or vegan dashi option was found.

chef_bio.background: Nitenmon Yabu is a long-established (老舗) soba shop that has stood at the Nitenmon Gate approach to Sensōji since 1954. The shop underwent a renovation (reported around 2017) that gave it a bright, modern concrete-and-glass exterior, though the interior is described as retaining the calm, unpretentious feel typical of an old Shitamachi (downtown) noodle shop.
chef_bio.specialty: Katsudon (pork cutlet over rice) — among Asakusa's soba-shop-style rice bowls, local food writers repeat the saying that for tempura rice bowl (tendon) you go to Owariya, and for katsudon you go to Nitenmon Yabu. The menu otherwise covers a standard range of soba, udon, donburi and drinking snacks.

anecdotes.text: Among Asakusa's soba-shop rice bowls, the local saying goes: for tendon (tempura rice bowl) it's Owariya, for katsudon it's Nitenmon Yabu — a nod to how well-regarded this shop's pork cutlet bowl is among old-school Asakusa soba restaurants.

The shop sits just east of Sensōji, right in front of the Nitenmon Gate, and was founded in 1954; despite a modern renovation with bare concrete walls, stepping inside reveals the calm atmosphere typical of a downtown (shitamachi) soba shop.

cultural_comfort.note: A cash-only, traditional neighborhood soba shop with no confirmed English menu; although it sits right at a major tourist landmark (Sensōji's Nitenmon Gate), ordering is likely easiest with a translation app or by pointing at photos.

Many plain roasted bean and nut items are inherently plant-based, but the broader 80+ item lineup (including sweetened, chocolate-coated, or novelty items like the MAMERON BAR) may contain honey, dairy (milk chocolate), or other animal-derived ingredients, and traditional Japanese confections can hide bonito/katsuo-derived seasonings. chef_bio.origin: Fukuyama, Hiroshima Prefecture
chef_bio.background: Mametoku traces back to 1869 (Meiji 2), when the Tokunaga family began in Fukuyama, Hiroshima as a grain and dried-goods merchant. The business shifted early on to focus on roasted bean snacks, and the shop took the name "Mametoku" (豆徳), combining mame (beans) with the Tokunaga family name of its founder, Tokunaga Shintarō. The Asakusa branch is one of several Mametoku locations run by the parent company, Tokunaga Seika Co. , Ltd. , and opened on December 21, 2020, in the Asakusa Shin-Nakamise shopping arcade, about a 3-minute walk from Sensō-ji's Kaminarimon (Thunder Gate).
chef_bio.philosophy: The company describes finishing its bean and nut confections by hand rather than relying solely on automated production, aiming to offer simple, everyday bean-based treats as part of a healthy diet, while continually developing new flavors alongside its traditional recipes.
chef_bio.specialty: Takezumi Mame (bamboo-charcoal-coated beans), developed in 2002, is the brand's longtime signature item. The Asakusa store additionally sells an exclusive item called "MAMERON BAR," a stick-shaped wafer topped with colorful roasted nuts.

anecdotes.text: 豆徳浅草店opened December 21, 2020, roughly a 3-minute walk from Sensō-ji's Kaminarimon (Raijin) Gate, inside the Asakusa Shin-Nakamise arcade, and is known locally for an Asakusa-exclusive item, the colorful nut-topped "MAMERON BAR."

The Mametoku name and business history date to 1869 in Fukuyama, Hiroshima, where the company (Tokunaga Seika Co., Ltd.) began as a grain merchant before specializing in bean confections; the shop name derives from founder Tokunaga Shintarō's surname combined with "mame" (beans).

cultural_comfort.note: It's a simple walk-up snack counter in a tourist-heavy shopping arcade — pointing at packaged bean and nut snacks and paying works fine even without Japanese, though staff may not speak much English.

tokyo_benizuru.gf_detail: The signature pancakes are made with rice flour (米粉) and kibi sugar instead of wheat flour and granulated sugar — this is the shop's core differentiator and is confirmed across many independent sources. However, no dedicated gluten-free kitchen, equipment, or wheat-free certification was found in any source; the menu also includes items such as waffles whose flour was not confirmed wheat-free, and sauces/toppings (hollandaise, marmalade) have unconfirmed ingredients. Treat this as "rice-flour-forward" rather than allergy-certified, and confirm cross-contact directly with staff if you have celiac disease.
tokyo_benizuru.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly: the signature dishes are built around bacon, fried eggs, hollandaise sauce (butter and egg yolk based), and honey as the standard sweetener across the pancake menu. No vegan alternative, plant-based substitution, or vegan-labeled item was found in any source.

The kitchen commonly sells out and closes before the nominal end time. Closed days are described as irregular (不定休) by most sources, though one blog specifies Wednesdays — unconfirmed.

chef_bio.origin: Before it was 紅鶴, this counter was a kissaten (old-style coffee shop) called "フラミンゴ" (Flamingo), run by the current owner's family in Asakusa for more than 50 years. In 2017 the owner, Makita-san, renewed the shop and renamed it 紅鶴 — which is simply the Japanese kanji word for "flamingo" — carrying the old shop's identity into its new pancake-focused form.
chef_bio.philosophy: Makita-san builds the pancakes around rice flour and kibi (raw cane) sugar instead of wheat flour and granulated sugar, and tops them with honey rather than maple syrup, aiming for a lighter batter that doesn't sit heavy in the stomach — his stated goal is a pancake that men, older customers and children can all enjoy comfortably, not just a dessert-cafe crowd.
chef_bio.specialty: Bacon and Fried Egg Pancake (ベーコンと目玉焼きのパンケーキ) — a three-layer soufflé-style rice-flour pancake stacked with honey, marmalade and bacon, topped with a fried egg and a generous pour of hollandaise sauce.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name and premise trace directly back to the owner's parents' decades-old kissaten "Flamingo," which he reopened as 紅鶴 (its kanji equivalent) in 2017 when he pivoted the menu to rice-flour pancakes.

The cafe drew a wave of new attention after being featured on the TV program 沸騰ワード10 in September 2025, with reports (and rumor) that Justin Bieber had eaten there alongside a long list of visiting Japanese celebrities.

gf_cross_contamination.text: FindMeGlutenFree listing: Benitsuru is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease; contact the establishment directly to inquire about safety precautions. No celiac-grade positive reviews present.
Waffles (ワッフル) are offered as a separate walk-in item; sources describe them without confirming rice flour, leaving wheat waffles as a plausible cross-contact source in the same small kitchen.

Allergen guidance: rice-flour products in Japan frequently contain blended wheat, Japan has no cross-contamination labeling obligation, and such products are often processed in rooms that also handle wheat — so 'made with rice flour' does not equal celiac-safe.

Signature dishes are built on bacon, fried egg, hollandaise sauce, marmalade and honey (e.g. 'Bacon and Fried Egg' ¥2,200 with honey, marmalade, bacon and hollandaise), with no vegan alternative — confirming vegan = no.

positives.text: The pancake batter itself is made with rice flour and kibi (raw cane) sugar rather than wheat flour and granulated sugar — described by the owner as a deliberate choice to make a lighter pancake that's easier to digest.

cultural_comfort.note: No English menu was confirmed and there is no phone/online booking — you must queue in person for a same-day numbered ticket, a distinctly Japanese-style system that is nonetheless well documented in English-language travel blogs and manageable if you arrive early and follow the queue etiquette.

tokyo_shabu_shabu_on_yasai_asa.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free menu or accommodation was found. The house dashi broths are the medium everything is cooked in, and the signature "Sandaime Kiwami Dashi" is explicitly built with soy sauce (a wheat-based white soy sauce), so wheat is present in the shared cooking liquid itself, not just in a separate dipping sauce — meaning even plain meat/vegetables cooked in it pick up gluten. A chain-wide allergen reference sheet is reportedly available on request, but shared pots and cooking equipment mean cross-contact is essentially unavoidable in the all-you-can-eat format. Not recommended for celiac diners without direct, specific confirmation from staff.
tokyo_shabu_shabu_on_yasai_asa.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly restaurant. The core menu is all-you-can-eat meat and vegetable shabu-shabu; the named default broths are fish-stock based (sardine, soda-bonito, mackerel), and even the soy-milk broth is finished with bonito and kombu dashi. A plain kombu (kelp-only) broth reportedly exists among the broth choices, which could in principle avoid animal-derived dashi, but no confirmed fully plant-based tare/dipping sauce or vegan protocol was found — a vegan diner would need to ask in detail and likely couldn't rely on any of the signature broths.
tokyo_shabu_shabu_on_yasai_asa.notes: Onyasai built its identity around vegetable-forward shabu-shabu: an all-you-can-eat format pairing thinly sliced meats with a large rotating selection of domestic vegetables, centered on a lineup of proprietary house-made dashi broths rather than a single generic soup base.

chef_bio.origin: National restaurant chain operated by Reins International (part of the Colowide group) — this is one branch (Asakusa) of the nationwide "Onyasai" vegetable shabu-shabu chain, not an independent or chef-owned establishment.
chef_bio.background: Onyasai built its identity around vegetable-forward shabu-shabu: an all-you-can-eat format pairing thinly sliced meats with a large rotating selection of domestic vegetables, centered on a lineup of proprietary house-made dashi broths rather than a single generic soup base.
chef_bio.specialty: All-you-can-eat vegetable and meat shabu-shabu with a choice of signature broths, most notably the "Sandaime Kiwami Dashi" (三代目極みだし), a seafood-based broth blending sardine, soda-bonito and mackerel with a white soy sauce.

anecdotes.text: For its 25th anniversary, the chain added two new proprietary dashi options to its grand menu — "Umi no Megumi Dashi" (a citrus-and-seafood broth) and "Awa-iro Ushio Dashi" (a sea bream and sea-salt broth) — continuing its broth-first approach to vegetable shabu-shabu.
The chain's signature broth, Sandaime Kiwami Dashi, is built from a fish-stock base of iwashi (sardine), soda-katsuo and saba (mackerel) finished with a premium white soy sauce.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The all-you-can-eat shabu-shabu format uses shared pots and cooking/washing equipment across meat and vegetable items, creating cross-contact risk for allergen-sensitive diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The chain's signature "Sandaime Kiwami Dashi" broth is built around a white soy sauce blended with sardine, soda-bonito and mackerel stock — soy sauce (and thus wheat) is in the base cooking liquid itself, not only in a side dipping sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The default/signature broths are fish-stock based (sardine, soda-katsuo, mackerel), and even the soy-milk broth option is cut with bonito and kombu dashi, so no broth on the standard menu is confirmed vegan; the restaurant's core product is all-you-can-eat meat shabu-shabu.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff can reportedly provide a printed 7-major-allergen reference sheet on request, but the chain notes shared cooking/washing equipment means cross-contamination cannot be ruled out.

positives.text: The chain is built around a large, frequently-rotating selection of domestic (国産) vegetables served alongside meat in an all-you-can-eat format, with several distinct proprietary broths to choose from.

cultural_comfort.note: A mainstream Japanese chain restaurant with no confirmed English menu or English-speaking staff, though its central Asakusa location (2 minutes from Asakusa Station) and an English Tabelog listing suggest some familiarity with tourists.

tokyo_kuroge_wagyu_ichinoya_as.gf_detail: The dish's signature "warishita" sauce is homemade from soy sauce (shoyu) and mirin — both typically contain wheat — and no gluten-free sauce alternative, dedicated fryer, or allergen-free protocol is mentioned anywhere. Because the menu is essentially one composed dish built on this sauce, there is no visible way to avoid wheat exposure. Treat as not safe for celiac/gluten-free diners without a direct, in-person conversation with staff (and even then, cross-contact risk in a tiny single-dish kitchen is likely high).
tokyo_kuroge_wagyu_ichinoya_as.vegan_detail: This is a single-specialty wagyu beef restaurant built entirely around a rare-steak rice bowl finished with an egg yolk and a beef-based dashi broth (hitsumabushi-style pour). No vegetarian or vegan preparation, substitute, or plant-based version of the signature dish was found in any source. Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.
tokyo_kuroge_wagyu_ichinoya_as.notes: [Mom & Pop] The shop's owner trained for eight years at a restaurant with roughly 260 years of history in Nihonbashi Ningyōchō before striking out to open their own place in Asakusa, wanting to share Japanese food culture and tradition through a single dish.

chef_bio.background: The shop's owner trained for eight years at a restaurant with roughly 260 years of history in Nihonbashi Ningyōchō before striking out to open their own place in Asakusa, wanting to share Japanese food culture and tradition through a single dish.
chef_bio.philosophy: Positioned as an evolution of Edo-period cuisine reimagined as a modern rice-bowl format, aiming to carry Japanese culinary tradition from Asakusa out into the world.
chef_bio.specialty: 黒毛和牛レアステーキ重 (Premium Rare Wagyu Steak Rice Bowl) — thin-sliced rare wagyu over rice, described as 'three flavors in one meal'.

anecdotes.text: Diners are guided through a three-stage way of eating the bowl: first plain to taste the meat and sauce, then mixed with a rich egg yolk, and finally finished hitsumabushi-style by pouring a beef dashi broth with condiments over the rice.
The shop has drawn continuous daily lines since its December 2022 opening and has been featured on Japanese gourmet TV (e.g. Hirunandesu!, Oct 2024).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house 'warishita' sauce is homemade from soy sauce and mirin — no gluten-free or wheat-free version is mentioned in any source found.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire menu centers on wagyu beef, egg yolk, and a beef-based dashi broth; no vegan, vegetarian, or plant-based option was found in any source.

cultural_comfort.note: Menu and service are Japanese-first with a queue-based, single-dish walk-in format typical of a small Asakusa specialty shop; expect to point/order simply rather than have detailed English allergy conversations.

No mention of a dedicated fryer (this is not a fried item) or of soy-sauce use. Confirm directly with staff before relying on this for celiac-level safety.
tokyo_warabimochi_motoko_asaku.vegan_detail: No vegan-specific statement from the shop was found. Kinako (soy flour) and kuromitsu (brown sugar syrup) used on plain warabi mochi are typically plant-based, but the shop's signature milk tea items are dairy-based (matcha/hōjicha/black tea milk teas), so those are not vegan as described unless a plant-milk substitute is confirmed in person. No information found on dashi/bonito use (unlikely relevant to a sweets shop, but unconfirmed).

anecdotes.text: The original わらび餅もとこ shop has been a beloved fixture in Sugamo, Tokyo for over 15 years; the Asakusa branch opened in December 2021 on the Nishi-Sandō approach street just west of Sensō-ji, and quickly became known for lines of customers.

The shop is credited with originating the 'warabi mochi milk tea' drink — chewy warabi-mochi pearls served in a milk tea (matcha, hōjicha, or black tea base, plus seasonal fruit punch versions) — alongside boat-shaped (fune-gata) fresh warabi mochi sold for eating while strolling Nishi-Sandō.
As of mid-2026 the Asakusa shop is operating from a temporary spot about one minute's walk from its usual address while its original location undergoes renovation.

cultural_comfort.note: It's a simple walk-up takeout/eat-in sweets counter near Sensō-ji with a picture-friendly menu of a handful of items, so pointing and ordering works fine even without Japanese, though menus and any staff conversation are likely Japanese-only.

Celiac-safe dining here cannot be confirmed and should not be assumed.

The menu otherwise centers on yakitori, horse sashimi, and motsu nabe (animal offal hot pot). No plant-based dashi/broth or dedicated vegan dishes were found in any source searched.

cultural_comfort.note: A Japanese-language neighborhood izakaya (net-reservation via Hot Pepper Gourmet) with no confirmed English menu or allergy-specific staff training, so non-Japanese-speaking diners with dietary restrictions should confirm ingredients in Japanese or bring a translation aid before ordering.

chef_bio.background: A closet-sized dim sum counter that opened in 2010 in a Nishi-Asakusa backstreet near the Kappabashi kitchenware district, a few minutes' walk from Tsukuba Express Asakusa Station. It's run out of a single storefront window with steam baskets fogging the glass, mostly by one owner at a five-stool counter, with a dim sum cook originally brought over from China making the dumplings.
chef_bio.philosophy: There's no fixed script here — write-ups describe an 'omakase' course that changes visit to visit depending on who's cooking and what's fresh, rather than a set menu recited the same way every time.
chef_bio.specialty: Thick-skinned pan-fried gyoza packed with cabbage, chives and pork, alongside shrimp and crab shumai, xiaolongbao and other bamboo-steamer dim sum, most of it priced around a flat 500 yen a plate.

anecdotes.text: A December 2024 blog visit found the tiny five-seat counter tucked in a backstreet near Kappabashi, steam rising from the shopfront window, serving thick-skinned pan-fried gyoza, shrimp-and-crab shumai and soup dumplings.

A Gurunavi feature on the shop's roughly 2,000-yen omakase course described a running joke among regulars: the more times you visit, the fewer dim sum dishes show up, because a second cook — a former Japanese-cuisine (washoku) chef who comes in some weekday evenings — keeps sneaking in seasonal, non-dim-sum dishes like simmered daikon with yellowtail and curry pork buns.

dancyu's 'Asakusa Lunch Guide' column ranked it 99th on a 100-spot list of the writer's favorite Asakusa lunches, describing a cramped five-stool room where dim sum is made by a chef the owner brought over from China, the shop having opened in 2010.

A gyoza-focused blog highlighted the lunch set — four pan-fried gyoza plus two shumai with rice and soup — priced at a flat 500 yen, calling out the unusually large amount of filling packed into each dumpling.

cultural_comfort.note: This reads as an old-school, Japanese-only backstreet counter with no evidence of English menus, picture menus, or foreign-visitor signage in any of the coverage found — come with at least basic Japanese or a translation app.

tokyo_asakusa_ikutaan.gf_detail: This shop is built entirely around housemade wheat noodles in a soy-sauce-based broth. No gluten-free noodle substitute, allergy menu, or any gluten-free accommodation was mentioned in any source found. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoidant diners.
tokyo_asakusa_ikutaan.vegan_detail: The broth is a rich animal-based stock (pork/chicken) topped with a layer of rendered lard, and the signature dishes are served with pork chashu. No vegetarian or vegan menu item was found in any source. Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.
tokyo_asakusa_ikutaan.hours_raw: 11:00–21:00 (Mon–Fri) and 10:00–21:00 (Sat, Sun, holidays) per one aggregated listing; other directories instead list a flat 11:00–23:00 and/or note irregular (不定休) closures. Sources disagree, so treat exact hours as approximate and confirm by phone if possible.
tokyo_asakusa_ikutaan.notes: [Mom & Pop] 生田庵 opened in February 2021 on Umamichi-dori near its intersection with Denpo-in-dori, a very short walk from Tobu Asakusa Station and the Kaminarimon/Sensoji area. It is a small, independently run counter-only shop rather than a chain.

chef_bio.background: 生田庵 opened in February 2021 on Umamichi-dori near its intersection with Denpo-in-dori, a very short walk from Tobu Asakusa Station and the Kaminarimon/Sensoji area. It is a small, independently run counter-only shop rather than a chain.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner has spoken of wanting to make it 'the best ramen shop in Asakusa' — the stated approach is to avoid gimmicks or showiness and instead stick to basic technique and orthodox, straightforward ingredients.
chef_bio.specialty: 中華そば (chuka-soba) — a soy-sauce-based ramen topped with a cap of rendered lard that keeps the broth hot throughout the meal, hand-sliced tender chashu pork, and housemade noodles; the shop also offers a spicy version and a cold dipping-noodle (tsukemen/mori-chuka) style.

anecdotes.text: The soup carries a layer of lard on its surface that keeps it hot from the first sip to the last, with each mouthful delivering salt, broth depth, and richness of fat together.
The owner has described the goal of becoming 'the best ramen shop in Asakusa,' keeping the shop unpretentious and built on simple, orthodox ingredients rather than novelty.

cultural_comfort.note: Order via a Japanese-only ticket vending machine at the entrance, typical of a small neighborhood ramen counter — no indication of English menus or English-speaking staff was found, so basic Japanese or pointing at the machine's photos/labels will help.

chef_bio.background: Asakusa Himurodo's Asakusa main branch opened in May 2023 in the Crest Asakusa building, a short walk from Asakusa Station. It is a dedicated kakigori (shaved ice) shop built around ice quality: the shop uses carefully selected, high-purity ice that is prized for melting almost instantly, giving the dessert what fans describe as a roughly "three-minute" window of peak texture before it's meant to be eaten.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on the purity of the ice itself and on natural, additive-free syrups made in-house, with menus that shift with the seasons to showcase fruit at its best.
chef_bio.specialty: Shaved ice topped with handmade syrups made without artificial colors, flavors, or sweeteners, built around seasonal fruit. Standouts include the fresh-strawberry kakigori and an Asakusa-location-exclusive ripe sweet potato (mitsuimo) kakigori, plus a version topped with real mitarashi dango.

anecdotes.text: The shop's ice is so fine and high-purity that it is said to have only about a three-minute window before it loses its ideal texture, a point of pride highlighted in visitor write-ups.
The Asakusa main store has a location-exclusive menu item, a fully ripened sweet potato (mitsuimo) shaved ice, alongside standards like fresh strawberry and a mitarashi-dango-topped version.

cultural_comfort.note: No English menu or English-speaking staff was confirmed in any source, though the shop sits in heavily-touristed Asakusa where some picture-menu/gesture communication is typical.

Even amid rising food prices, the restaurant has been noted for holding the line on its budget-friendly lunch pricing (lunches under 1,000 yen).

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, one-woman-run neighborhood Thai spot in the heart of Asakusa — simple, friendly interactions are easy, but don't expect an English menu or extensive English-speaking staff.

chef_bio.background: "Chiisana Kankoku Apuro" (小さな韓国あぷろ, literally "Little Korea Apuro") is a Korean-cuisine restaurant chain founded in Fukuoka in 2010, during the second wave of the Korean cultural boom in Japan (the era of K-pop acts like KARA and BIGBANG breaking into the Japanese market). Run by the company (有)あぷろ under representative 水本尚宏, the chain has grown to roughly 20 locations, mostly around Fukuoka but extending into the Kansai and Kanto regions, including this Shibuya branch on Dogenzaka near Shinsen Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: The restaurant's stated approach is to bring authentic Korean culture, not just food, to Japan: ingredients are sourced domestically or from Korea, and seasonings and kimchi are made in-house. The Shibuya branch leans into the K-pop/Korean-wave aesthetic, pairing an open-kitchen street-food-stall style ground floor with a second-floor space built around large screens and K-pop music videos for a more immersive, party-oriented atmosphere.
chef_bio.specialty: Thick-cut samgyeopsal (grilled pork belly) using pork from the Kirishima foothills, grilled tableside by staff, alongside apuro's signature pajeon (Korean savory pancakes).

anecdotes.text: The chain opened in 2010 during the second Korean Wave (Hallyu) boom in Japan and has since expanded to about 20 locations centered on Fukuoka, reaching into the Kanto and Kansai regions.

The Shibuya store's 1st floor is built around an open kitchen and vivid drum-can (street-stall style) tables, while the 2nd floor is a K-pop-themed space with a large screen and jukebox for a livelier, party atmosphere.

cultural_comfort.note: A Japan-based Korean-food chain in a busy Shibuya nightlife street; no confirmed English menu or English-speaking staff, so expect a standard Japanese-language dining experience with some English via ordering apps/QR menus common at similar izakaya-style chains.

chef_bio.background: Trois Bagues Vertes is the second location of Café Trois Bagues, a Jimbocho kissaten (Japanese-style coffee shop) that has been running since 1976. The name plays on the founding family's surname, Miwa (三輪): in French, trois means 'three' and bague means 'ring,' echoing the kanji 輪 ('ring') in Miwa. The original café is now run by second-generation owner Tokuko Miwa. In June 2024 the family opened this second branch a short walk away in Kanda Sarugakucho, near Suidobashi, decorated with a pale-green ('vertes') ceiling, antique furniture, and plants.
chef_bio.specialty: Gratin crepe and Crepe Pudding à la Mode, paired with nel-drip (flannel filter) coffee

anecdotes.text: Staff member Midorikawa-san explained that crepes were chosen for the new shop simply because there was no dedicated crepe shop in the Jimbocho area at the time.
The signature gratin crepe wraps the same béchamel-based gratin used in the original café's famous gratin toast, topped with tomato sauce and cheese and baked.
The shop name Trois Bagues is a play on the founding family's surname Miwa (三輪): trois (three) + bague (ring), echoing the kanji 輪 ('ring').

cultural_comfort.note: A retro, Japanese-style kissaten café with no confirmed English menu or English-speaking service found in any source, so plan for ordering in Japanese.

No cross-contamination protocol or celiac-specific information was found in available sources. Ask staff directly about ingredients before ordering if you need strict gluten-free food.

chef_bio.background: Kayu Sanchin (粥餐庁) is a Chinese/Taiwanese-style congee (okayu) and noodle specialty chain. The brand's operations were transferred to Green House Foods Co. , Ltd. (a major Tokyo-based food-service company headquartered in Nishi-Shinjuku) in 2008, and it now runs multiple branches, including this one tucked into the underground Keio Mall passage directly connected to Shinjuku Station's south exit / west exit area.
chef_bio.philosophy: Positioned as a healthy, comforting meal for busy commuters — porridge made with a white-rice and brown-rice blend, served from early morning (7am on weekdays) through late evening, with abundant vegetable and protein toppings to choose from.
chef_bio.specialty: Congee (rice porridge) made from a white-and-brown rice blend, with topping options such as Taiwanese-style braised pork (lu rou), plum, steamed chicken, shrimp with cheese and tomato, and a multi-vegetable congee (lotus root, daikon, sweet potato, broccoli, cherry tomato, etc. ); the shop's special tantan noodles are also a recommended item.

anecdotes.text: A long-running, popular spot inside Keio Mall where lines form at lunchtime for its rice-blend congee.
Open as early as 7:00am on weekdays, making it one of the few sit-down 'proper meal' options near Shinjuku Station before the morning commute rush.

positives.text: Menu includes a dedicated multi-vegetable congee option with toppings such as lotus root, daikon, sweet potato, broccoli, and cherry tomato, giving vegetarian-leaning diners a clear plant-forward choice.

cultural_comfort.note: The shop's listing indicates menu/signage support for English, Chinese, and Korean in addition to Japanese, and it's a well-trafficked spot inside a major station mall, so ordering should be manageable for non-Japanese-speaking visitors.

tokyo_maruhashi.gf_detail: No gluten-free preparation, 100%-buckwheat (juwari) noodle, or dedicated fryer is advertised anywhere in the sources found. As a standard machi-soba shop, the soba is very likely a wheat-blended (nihachi-style) noodle, and the tsuyu dipping sauce/broth almost certainly relies on wheat-based shoyu; the tendon is deep-fried tempura, with no mention of a separate gluten-free fryer. Not recommended for celiac diners.
tokyo_maruhashi.vegan_detail: No vegan menu or option is advertised. As a traditional soba shop, the dashi/broth used for the tsuyu and soups is very likely katsuobushi (bonito)-based, and the tendon batter/frying is standard tempura preparation — not suitable for vegan diners without direct, in-person confirmation (in Japanese) from staff.
tokyo_maruhashi.hours_raw: Sources conflict: one listing gives Mon-Sat 11:00-16:00 (closed Sun/holidays); a more detailed listing gives Mon-Fri 11:30-15:00 & 17:00-19:00, Sat 11:30-15:00 (closed Sun/holidays). The record below uses the more detailed split-hours version but this should be confirmed by phone (03-3407-1212).
tokyo_maruhashi.notes: [Mom & Pop] This Shibuya branch sits down a back alley off the main road near Shibuya's south/east side, marked by a soba sign and blue noren, and has long been a lunchtime fixture for nearby office workers rather than a destination restaurant. · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).

chef_bio.origin: The Maruhashi soba lineage traces to a shop founded in Ueno Hirokoji in Taisho 7 (1918); a second-generation owner opened what became the main store in Gakugeidaigaku in 1956, from which roughly a dozen branches (including this Higashi/Shibuya shop, near Namiki-bashi) spread across Tokyo and Kanagawa over the following decades.
chef_bio.background: This Shibuya branch sits down a back alley off the main road near Shibuya's south/east side, marked by a soba sign and blue noren, and has long been a lunchtime fixture for nearby office workers rather than a destination restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: A no-frills neighborhood soba shop (machi-soba) valued for consistency, affordability, and the quiet pride of an old-school local counter rather than any modern reinvention.
chef_bio.specialty: Tendon (tempura rice bowl), about ¥900, served with miso soup and pickles; also mori/kake/tempura soba from about ¥450 and udon.

anecdotes.text: A local food blog titled its writeup 'A shop with the pride of a neighborhood soba restaurant,' describing hearty, reasonably priced soba and tendon served in a modest, workaday setting near Shibuya station.

An article on the wider Maruhashi lineage recounts the shop's roots to a 1918 Ueno founding and traces how the family's soba shops, including this Shibuya branch, spread through the city over roughly a century.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional, cash-only neighborhood soba counter with no indication of an English menu or English-speaking staff — expect to order in Japanese from a printed menu or wall signage.

tokyo_bodaiju.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu, substitutions, or accommodations were found in any source. tokyo_bodaiju.vegan_detail: No vegetarian or vegan menu items, substitutions, or accommodations were found. The menu is centered on wagyu beef hamburg steak and pork tonkatsu, both meat-based dishes; sauces (demi-glace) are typically meat-stock based in this style of cooking, though not explicitly confirmed. Not suitable for vegan diners based on available information.

chef_bio.background: Bodaiju has been serving hearty Western-style (yōshoku) comfort food near Suidōbashi Station for more than four decades. It operates under the same restaurant group as Katsuyoshi (かつ吉), a historic tonkatsu specialist founded in 1962, and shares that group's focus on hand-made fried and grilled classics.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen states a commitment to hand-making everything from fresh ingredients and avoiding additives and preservatives.
chef_bio.specialty: A5 wagyu hamburg steak (A5和牛ハンバーグ) — fresh A5-grade Japanese wagyu ground in-house, formed into hamburg patties, and slow-simmered in a house-made demi-glace sauce; also known for traditional tonkatsu made with daily-sourced branded domestic pork wrapped in fresh panko and slow-fried in a corn-and-sesame oil blend.

anecdotes.text: The A5 wagyu hamburger lunch set is limited to roughly 20 servings a day and has built a devoted following among lunchtime regulars.
Beyond the hamburg and tonkatsu, regulars are said to come specifically for the shiso gohan (perilla-leaf rice), a labor-intensive side dish that has become something of a hidden signature.
The dining room is described as wood-toned with brick walls and jazz playing throughout, giving the space an unhurried, old-school yōshoku atmosphere.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature tonkatsu is coated in fresh wheat panko and fried in a shared corn-salad-oil and sesame-oil blend used across the fried menu; no gluten-free fryer or breading alternative was identified in any source.

cultural_comfort.note: All sources found are Japanese-language (menu, reservation site, blogs); no English menu or English-speaking service was confirmed, so bring a translation tool for any allergy conversation.

tokyo_tori_soba_mitaba.gf_detail: No gluten-free noodle option or allergen protocol was found in any source. The noodles are standard wheat ramen noodles, and the tare/seasoning is not confirmed wheat-free. Not recommended for celiac diners.
tokyo_tori_soba_mitaba.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian broth option was found. The signature and apparently only broth style offered is a rich chicken paitan (鶏白湯) built from chicken bones/collagen, which is inherently non-vegan; dashi/bonito use in any secondary items is not documented either way.
tokyo_tori_soba_mitaba.notes: [Mom & Pop] The shop is run by a female owner-chef who trained under the well-known ramen brand Menya Buichi (麺屋武一) before striking out on her own; the counter is staffed by a mostly female crew, which multiple diner write-ups call out as unusual for a Kabukicho late-night ramen shop. · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).

chef_bio.background: The shop is run by a female owner-chef who trained under the well-known ramen brand Menya Buichi (麺屋武一) before striking out on her own; the counter is staffed by a mostly female crew, which multiple diner write-ups call out as unusual for a Kabukicho late-night ramen shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: Positioned as an easy, unintimidating late-night stop in Kabukicho — open from late morning straight through to 6am — welcoming solo diners (including women) into a nightlife district where that isn't always the norm.
chef_bio.specialty: 特製濃厚鶏白湯 (Tokusei Nokou Tori-Paitan) — a rich, collagen-heavy chicken paitan broth served with thin noodles; described by reviewers as creamy and full-bodied but not heavy.

A ramen-focused blog notes the shop is known for chicken-centered bowls spanning rich tori-paitan, lighter clear broths, and Jiro-inspired styles.
Reviewers on Retty specifically highlight that the owner and staff are women running a chicken-paitan specialist in the heart of Kabukicho.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, all-Japanese neighborhood ramen counter in Kabukicho with no evidence of an English menu, so a little Japanese (or pointing at photos/the Tabelog menu) goes a long way.

tokyo_asakusa_chisou_nishizawa.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu, statement, or allergy policy was found on any source. As a traditional Japanese kaiseki restaurant, the omakase course very likely relies on soy sauce and dashi (both commonly containing wheat/gluten and bonito-derived ingredients), and may include tempura or breaded items. There is no evidence of a dedicated gluten-free fryer or wheat-free soy sauce. Celiac diners should call ahead (050-8881-7620) to discuss the course in detail before booking.
tokyo_asakusa_chisou_nishizawa.vegan_detail: No vegan menu or accommodation was found. The omakase is built around sashimi, charcoal-grilled fish/meat, and clay-pot rice made with seasonal fish, and likely uses bonito (katsuo) dashi throughout — there is no indication the kitchen offers a plant-based course or can rework the set menu to remove fish/dashi.
tokyo_asakusa_chisou_nishizawa.notes: Asakusa Chisou Nishizawa (浅草馳走にし座わ) opened on July 17, 2024 in Asakusa. chef_bio.background: Asakusa Chisou Nishizawa (浅草馳走にし座わ) opened on July 17, 2024 in Asakusa. According to information associated with the restaurant's Instagram account, the chef previously worked at establishments in both Asakusa and Ginza before opening this restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: A seasonal, chef's-choice (omakase) course built around whatever ingredients are best at the time of the visit, served in a calm, refined room alongside a curated selection of Shizuoka-prefecture sake.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small, reservation-only Japanese omakase restaurant booked mainly through Japanese platforms (Hot Pepper, Autoreserve, Tabelog Japanese site); no evidence of an English menu or English-speaking staff was found, so some Japanese ability or a hotel/concierge booking will help.

tokyo_menya_tori_roji.gf_detail: Standard ramen shop using conventional wheat noodles and a soy-sauce (shoyu) broth base; no gluten-free noodle substitute, dedicated gluten-free preparation, or allergen accommodation was found in any source. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.

chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's name, Tori Roji (鶏路地), is a pun on the Japanese pronunciation of 'trilogy' (torirojii) — a nod to its concept of three chicken-broth ramen styles built from one base stock.
chef_bio.specialty: Tori paitan (creamy, slow-simmered all-chicken broth) ramen, offered in three versions: shoyu, shio, and tantan.

anecdotes.text: The counter is run by a single, quiet ('taciturn') male operator, giving the shop the low-key, no-frills character typical of Tokyo's small hole-in-the-wall ramen counters.

cultural_comfort.note: A local walk-in ramen counter run by one operator with no confirmed English menu or English-speaking staff on site; ordering will likely require some Japanese or menu-pointing, though Tabelog offers an English-language listing for reference.

tokyo_mamekobo_suidobashi_self.gf_detail: Straight black/drip coffee is inherently gluten-free, but no gluten-free labeling, dedicated equipment, or specific allergen information was found for the food items sold here (e.g., handmade sandwiches, baked goods). tokyo_mamekobo_suidobashi_self.vegan_detail: Plain black/drip coffee is vegan. chef_bio.background: Mamekobo (豆香房) is a self-roasting specialty coffee company with a small group of shops in the Kanda/Suidobashi area of Chiyoda-ku. The Suidobashi branch is a small, traditional coffee-shop-style café a short walk from the station, built around beans the company roasts itself.
chef_bio.philosophy: The roastery uses small-scale roasting machines rather than large industrial ones so each batch can be controlled delicately to bring out the individual character of the beans, and beans are sold/served only within about five days of roasting. The shop is a member of the Japan Specialty Coffee Association.
chef_bio.specialty: In-house roasted specialty coffee — the drip coffee on offer rotates through different single-origin and micro-lot beans up to three times a day (morning, midday, afternoon).

anecdotes.text: The company roasts specialty micro-lot and rare coffee lots in-house on small-batch roasters for delicate flavor control, and is a member of the Japan Specialty Coffee Association.
The coffee selection changes up to three times a day (morning, midday, and afternoon), and all beans sold are roasted within the previous five days.

cultural_comfort.note: Small, locals-oriented specialty coffee shop near Suidobashi Station with no confirmed English menu or signage; basic Japanese or a translation app will help when ordering.

tokyo_menya_kaijin_shinjuku.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodations found. The custom noodles are made from a blend of two wheat flours (小麦粉/domestic wheat flour, starch, salt, egg white/kansui per ingredient listings), and toppings such as shrimp tsumire and chicken tsukune also contain wheat. No dedicated gluten-free menu, wheat-free soy sauce, or dedicated fryer was found; celiac diners should not eat here.
tokyo_menya_kaijin_shinjuku.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The signature and essentially only broth is made from grilled fish bones/heads (about seven kinds of fresh fish, varying daily), and standard toppings include shrimp tsumire (fish/shrimp meatballs) and chicken tsukune. No plant-based broth or vegan menu option was found.
tokyo_menya_kaijin_shinjuku.notes: A long-running specialty salt-ramen shop just steps from Shinjuku Station's southeast exit, currently run by owner Endo Etsuko. chef_bio.background: A long-running specialty salt-ramen shop just steps from Shinjuku Station's southeast exit, currently run by owner Endo Etsuko. When it opened, there were no other ramen shops in the immediate area, which at the time was known more as an adult nightlife district.
chef_bio.philosophy: Because the fish delivered each morning changes, the soup's exact flavor shifts day to day — guests are invited to enjoy those daily variations rather than a fixed recipe. The noodles are a custom blend of two wheat flours, thin but firm enough to stand up to the broth.
chef_bio.specialty: あら炊き塩らぁめん (grilled fish-bone salt ramen) — broth made by first flame-searing the bones and heads of about seven kinds of fresh fish (varies daily, e. g. sea bream, yellowtail) and then simmering them slowly, carefully skimming impurities for a clean, concentrated seafood flavor without any fishy edge.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free menu or process was found; noodles and multiple toppings contain wheat, so cross-contamination is essentially unavoidable in this kitchen.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is fish-bone based (grilled fish scraps) and toppings include shrimp and chicken, so there is no vegan-safe base at this shop.

cultural_comfort.note: A local specialty ramen shop with Japanese-only signage and menu conventions typical of Tokyo counter ramen shops; no English menu was confirmed.

Thai and Vietnamese kitchens routinely season vegetable dishes and broths with fish sauce, oyster sauce, or shrimp paste, and soups may use non-vegan stock, so strict vegans should ask specifically for dishes made without fish sauce, oyster sauce, and shrimp paste rather than assuming any vegetable dish is automatically vegan.

chef_bio.background: Saamrot has served Thai and Vietnamese food in Kabukicho for more than two decades, tucked in the alleys between the Golden Gai nightlife strip and Hanazono Shrine. It has been recognized by Thailand's Ministry of Commerce / Thai Select as a restaurant serving authentic Thai cuisine.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name Saamrot means "three tastes" in Thai, referring to the sweet, spicy, and sour balance that Thai cooking is built around.
chef_bio.specialty: Gapao (Thai basil stir-fry) rice served in several versions — beef, pork, seafood, black tiger prawn — plus a tom yum kung the restaurant is known for locally.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant's tom yum kung is described as having earned top marks from all five judges on a Thai-food television competition.
The name Saamrot ("three tastes") refers to the sweet-spicy-sour balance that anchors the kitchen's approach to Thai cooking.
The restaurant sits on the second floor of a mixed-use building in an alley between Kabukicho's Golden Gai and Hanazono Shrine, with a compact, low-lit dining room of around 30 table seats.

positives.text: The menu includes vegetable-forward dishes such as stir-fried mixed vegetables and morning glory (kang kong / water spinach) alongside the standard Thai and Vietnamese offerings.

cultural_comfort.note: Tabelog maintains an English-language listing and the restaurant is used to Kabukicho's mixed foreign/local nightlife crowd, but no English menu or English-speaking staff was confirmed, so a few basic Japanese phrases will help.

tokyo_gluten_free_cafe_avan_sh.gf_detail: The shop states it uses no wheat flour anywhere on the menu, substituting rice flour (Yamagata Shonai "Haenuki" rice) even in savory items like fried chicken and taco rice, which is why it markets itself as a gluten-free specialty shop. However, this is described in sources as a "no wheat flour" commitment rather than a certified strict celiac protocol: at least one English-language celiac reviewer reported becoming ill after the taco rice and cautioned that hidden gluten sources (e.g., wheat in soy sauce/seasonings used in savory dishes) may not be fully screened, and that the shop's definition of "gluten-free" may lean toward "wheat-free." Sweets/churros are more consistently reported as safe than the savory menu. Celiac travelers should ask specifically about soy sauce, dashi, and seasoning ingredients before ordering savory items.
tokyo_gluten_free_cafe_avan_sh.vegan_detail: The core menu (rice-flour churros, fried chicken, taco rice) is not vegan by default, as it includes meat and likely dairy/egg in some sweets. However, sources note the shop offers seasonal vegan-and-gluten-free-compatible desserts, such as a shaved ice made with homemade almond cream and soy milk cream instead of condensed milk, indicating some deliberate vegan-friendly options exist alongside the main gluten-free-focused menu. Vegan diners should ask about egg/dairy in specific baked goods and about hidden animal-derived seasonings (e.g., dashi, bonito) in savory dishes, which were not specifically documented in available sources.
tokyo_gluten_free_cafe_avan_sh.hours_raw: 月・水・木・金・土・日 11:00-21:00（ラストオーダー 20:30）、火曜定休。一部情報源では第2・第3木曜日も休みとの記載あり（要確認）。

chef_bio.origin: 渋谷区神泉（Shinsen, Shibuya）
chef_bio.background: GLUTEN FREE CAFE avanは、小麦粉を一切使わず、山形県庄内産の米（はえぬき）を丁寧に製粉した米粉だけで作るグルテンフリー専門店として神泉駅近くにオープン。 渋谷本店はブランドの中心となる店舗で、後に上野エキュートなど他店舗も展開している。
chef_bio.philosophy: 「小麦を使わない」ことを店全体で徹底し、スイーツだけでなく総菜メニュー（唐揚げ、タコライスなど）まで含めて小麦粉不使用にこだわることで、グルテンに配慮したい人が安心して選べる場を目指している。
chef_bio.specialty: 米粉チュロス（Rice flour churros）— 山形県庄内産の極細挽き米粉と米油を使い、外はサクサク、中はもちもちの食感に仕上げた看板メニュー。 フレーバー展開も豊富。

anecdotes.text: 「チュロスがやみつきになるグルテンフリーカフェ、神泉『avan 渋谷本店』」として紹介され、米粉チュロスの食感と味が高く評価されている。
米粉タイムズ等のグルメメディアでも、山形県庄内産のブランド米「はえぬき」を極細挽きした米粉を使用したチュロスとして紹介されている。

Another reviewer, noting it functions as a dedicated gluten-free facility, said staff seemed confident about what they could serve even with a language barrier, rating the experience positively (5 stars).

A reviewer reported becoming ill after having the taco rice and noted that, based on the shop's website, they seem to think 'gluten-free' only equals 'wheat free,' cautioning those with Celiac to be careful.

chef_bio.origin: Shinjuku, Tokyo
chef_bio.background: Founded in Taisho 4 (1915), in the middle of World War I, near what would become Shinjuku Station's southeast exit. The building has been rebuilt twice since — it burned down during World War II and was rebuilt, and the current building dates to the postwar high-growth era when Naganoya came to own the property outright — making it a rare shokudo with over a century of continuous history steps from one of the world's busiest train stations.
chef_bio.philosophy: A working-class daily-use shokudo (cafeteria) rather than a destination restaurant — cheap, filling teishoku served fast to office workers, regulars, and the occasional daytime drinker, preserving a Showa-era dining atmosphere just steps from the ultramodern station.
chef_bio.specialty: 肉どうふ (nikudofu) — beef and tofu simmered until dark brown in a sweet-savory soy broth, served with rice and miso soup; also known for katsudon and katsu curry

anecdotes.text: Naganoya was founded in Taisho 4 (1915), amid World War I, and has weathered Shinjuku's constant redevelopment around it ever since; the current building is the third to stand on the site, rebuilt after wartime fire damage and again during the postwar economic boom.

The signature nikudofu (meat and tofu) is simmered until dark brown, the tofu soaking up the soy-based broth for a balance of saltiness and sweetness that pairs well with a drink; it comes with a miso soup containing tofu and seaweed.
Walking in feels like stepping into the Showa era — a woman greets guests at the counter while regulars sit quietly reading the newspaper, just one minute from Shinjuku Station's southeast exit.

cultural_comfort.note: A century-old neighborhood shokudo with handwritten menus and a regulars-only feel — no English menu was found in any source, so basic Japanese or pointing at the menu board will help.

chef_bio.origin: Tokyo (chef born 1964, per his own public profile)
chef_bio.background: Kaemon opened as an organic restaurant near Asakusa Station built around a self-described "food barrier-free" (食のバリアフリー) concept: a menu meant to be safely enjoyed by guests of any nationality, religion, or dietary restriction. It is run by owner-chef Uehara Kazunori, who has described publicly moving toward extreme minimal eating ("breatharian"-style, at most one meal a day, sometimes weeks without food) since around 2014 while continuing to develop the restaurant's menu. The current flagship (本店) location is on the 3rd floor of a building called AUSPICE in Hanakawado, a couple of minutes from Asakusa Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: "Food barrier-free" dining: no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy, plus deliberate avoidance of the five pungent alliums (onion, garlic, scallion, Chinese chive, shallot) used in Buddhist shojin cooking, so the restaurant calls its cuisine "Oriental Vegetarian. " The kitchen sources seasonal organic produce and reworks the menu around whatever arrives.
chef_bio.specialty: Soba-flour and organic wheat pancake (そば粉と有機小麦のパンケーキ), a long-running signature item; also a rotating organic-vegetable buffet and set courses ("かえもんディナーセット", "旬の厳選野菜コース")

anecdotes.text: The restaurant's stated aim is to be a "food barrier-free" restaurant so that people can eat without worry regardless of nationality or religion, avoiding onion, garlic, and leek in addition to meat, fish, egg, and dairy.

Produce is sourced from an organic farm in Chiba ("Hyakushou Farm"), and the kitchen aims to develop around 300 new menu items a year, testing new dishes daily to match whatever seasonal vegetables arrive.

Hall manager Imai Masafumi, interviewed by Meat Free Monday All Japan, described Kaemon's cuisine as built on shojin (Buddhist temple cooking) principles with the five-allium restriction, and said the restaurant also runs a volunteer "Fairy System" where helpers are compensated in an internal currency called "MON" rather than as conventional employees.

Owner Uehara Kazunori has publicly described becoming increasingly able to go without food after time spent traveling in mountainous regions, adopting a very-low-food ("breatharian") lifestyle from around 2014 while continuing to run the restaurant's kitchen.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen does not prepare meat, fish, egg, or dairy dishes at all — it is a fully plant-based operation, and miso soup/broths reportedly use a vegetable-scrap broth ("vege broth") instead of bonito-based dashi.

positives.text: Restaurant explicitly markets itself as "food barrier-free," avoiding meat, fish, egg, dairy, and the five pungent alliums (onion, garlic, scallion, Chinese chive, shallot) so that diners with a range of dietary and religious restrictions can eat there.
Listed on Vegewel's curated directory of vegetarian/vegan/gluten-free-friendly restaurants near Asakusa Station.

cultural_comfort.note: The restaurant appears on English-language Tabelog and halal/vegan tourist directories aimed at foreign visitors, suggesting some accommodation for non-Japanese speakers, but the on-site level of spoken English was not confirmed from available sources.

tokyo_hinai_komachi_shibuya.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu or allergy protocol was found. Yakitori here is typically offered either tare-glazed (a soy-based sauce that contains wheat) or shio (salt-grilled, no soy sauce) — shio-style skewers would be the safer ask, but cross-contact on a shared charcoal grill and in shared sauces/marinades is unconfirmed either way. The signature kiritanpo nabe hot pot uses a chicken-based dashi broth whose full seasoning (soy sauce, etc.) is not documented. Celiac diners should not assume safety without asking staff directly and should not rely on this listing alone.
tokyo_hinai_komachi_shibuya.vegan_detail: This is a chicken (Hinai-jidori) specialty izakaya; there is no vegan or vegetarian menu. Vegetable yakitori skewers (野菜串) exist as individual items, but they are grilled on the same charcoal grill as meat skewers and the restaurant's signature broths (e.g., kiritanpo nabe) are chicken-stock based, so hidden animal-derived dashi/stock is likely throughout the menu. Not a suitable choice for strict vegans; only worth considering for flexible vegetarians willing to ask detailed questions about individual vegetable items.

chef_bio.origin: Amagasaki, Hyogo Prefecture (founder's hometown)
chef_bio.background: Founder Masataka Aihara was born in 1972 in Amagasaki, Hyogo Prefecture. He moved to Tokyo at age 22 originally aiming to become an actor, but ended up joining a major seafood company, where he quickly rose to store manager and buyer. He later worked as a "fish concierge," supplying seafood to major supermarket chains and running tuna-breakdown demonstration events to boost sales. In 2004 he founded Takamaru Co. , Ltd. and obtained a Tsukiji market trading license, running wholesale and retail-training contracts. Unsatisfied with fixed annual contracts that were not tied to results, he founded Takamaru Sengyoten in 2009 to test his own sales ability directly through retail and restaurant operation.
chef_bio.philosophy: Steady, word-of-mouth growth rather than flashy advertising: the first shop opened in 2009 in a converted 18-tsubo garage; as regulars increased and space ran short, the company opened additional branches within walking distance rather than expanding aggressively.

anecdotes.text: The provocative shop name itself doubles as an advertisement — its odd phrasing ("Why do you put chili oil in soba?") sparks curiosity and has become a talking point that drives customers to try it.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual local chain soba shop near Shibuya Station; no evidence of an English menu or English-speaking staff, so basic Japanese or pointing at the menu/photos will help when ordering.

chef_bio.philosophy: Follows AVPN's traditional Neapolitan pizza discipline: the wood-fired oven was hand-built by Stefano Ferrara, a master oven craftsman from Naples, using stone and sand shipped in from Naples itself. chef_bio.specialty: Wood-fired Neapolitan pizza — the classic Margherita (tomato, mozzarella, basil) and the cheese-free Marinara (tomato, garlic, oregano, olive oil), plus a house Americana topped with capers, corn, pepperoni, paprika, red onion and cherry tomatoes. Most pizzas can be ordered half-and-half so diners can try two varieties at once.

roles: Restaurant brand of Food Supply Co., a Tokyo-based vegetable wholesaler
chef_bio.origin: Founded by Food Supply Co., a produce (vegetable) wholesaler run by president Atsushi Takekawa (born 1979, Tottori), who founded the company in 2009.
chef_bio.background: During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Takekawa launched a contact-free 'drive-through vegetable stand' to sell produce directly to consumers after many of the company's restaurant clients closed and growers lost their usual buyers. That effort became the foundation for Vejiro, a meat-and-vegetable stir-fry restaurant designed to move large volumes of fresh vegetables and support the producers who had been left with unsold crops. The Shibuya main store (総本店) opened near Bunkamura in Dogenzaka in December 2021 and quickly became one of Shibuya's most talked-about lunch/dinner spots, known for long lines.
chef_bio.philosophy: Turn a produce wholesaler's surplus-vegetable problem into a restaurant concept — build a dish that lets one diner eat a very large quantity of vegetables in a single sitting, giving growers a reliable outlet for their harvest.
chef_bio.specialty: 肉野菜炒め定食 (meat & vegetable stir-fry set meal), Jiro-ramen-inspired: a mountain of stir-fried vegetables (customers can order it 'mashi-mashi', with reports of roughly 400g of vegetables per plate) tossed with sliced pork or fried chicken, seasoned with a choice of soy sauce, miso, ponzu, or salt-tonkotsu, and topped with an adjustable amount of pork back fat.

anecdotes.text: A single plate is built around roughly 400g of stir-fried vegetables — described as close to a full day's recommended vegetable intake in one meal.
The restaurant grew directly out of Takekawa's pandemic-era 'drive-through vegetable shop,' created after Food Supply's restaurant clients shut down and growers lost their delivery destinations.

positives.text: The menu includes a vegetables-only order (no meat), for diners who want a plant-forward version of the stir-fry.
The restaurant was created specifically to serve unusually large portions of fresh vegetables per plate, sourced through the operator's own produce-wholesale business.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering happens via a Japanese-language customization system (rice, sauce, vegetable/fat quantity) at a small, often-crowded counter, so basic Japanese or pointing at the menu board helps.

chef_bio.background: Niku Bistro Akari opened in the backstreets of Nishi-Shinjuku 7-chome as a new meat-and-wine concept from Zekkocho (株式会社絶好調), the Shinjuku izakaya group led by Masaki Yoshida (of Zekkocho Teppen), built around pairing whole block meat seared over charcoal with a locked, lantern-lit wine cellar guests browse themselves.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than chasing famous meat brands, the kitchen selects cuts by season and quality, rotating 6-8 different kinds of block meat daily and searing them hard over binchotan charcoal so the centers stay rare and juicy.
chef_bio.specialty: Block meat -- beef, pork, lamb, and game such as venison and wild boar -- grilled whole over binchotan charcoal and served rare and juicy, alongside a hand-picked cellar of about 150 wines.

anecdotes.text: Diners choose their own bottle by stepping into a key-locked, lantern-lit wine cellar stocked with roughly 150 red, white, and sparkling wines.

The kitchen rotates 6-8 kinds of block meat a day -- from standard beef, pork, and lamb to game like venison and wild boar -- chosen for seasonality and quality rather than brand name, then seared hard over binchotan charcoal.
Meats such as Kumamoto 'aka-gyu' beef and Iwate pork are grilled over roaring binchotan charcoal and brought to the table as showstopping platters.
The restaurant opened on July 7 in Nishi-Shinjuku 7-chome as a new bone-in-meat-and-wine concept from Zekkocho Teppen founder Masaki Yoshida.

chef_bio.background: Saeki graduated from Dokkyo University's Faculty of Foreign Languages (English Department) and worked in administrative roles before turning toward food around 2005. In 2012 she co-opened a shizen-saibai (naturally-cultivated, pesticide- and fertilizer-free) vegetable restaurant, and in January 2020 she opened Vegan Cafe Monkey Magic in a quiet alley behind Hanayashiki in Asakusa, on the ground floor of a small inn called Oyado Matsumura.
chef_bio.philosophy: Saeki was vegan herself for several years but stepped back from strict veganism for health reasons; she says she now channels that firsthand experience into cooking she describes as 'vegan food that nourishes the heart,' built entirely on naturally cultivated vegetables and natural fermentation seasonings with no additives.
chef_bio.specialty: A monthly-changing, multi-course tasting menu (including a seasonal vegan take on sushi) built around 100% naturally cultivated vegetables and house-made fermented seasonings.

anecdotes.text: Once vegan herself, Saeki quit strict veganism for health reasons and has used that perspective to create what she calls 'vegan food that nourishes the heart' rather than just the body.

It has since grown into one of Tokyo's largest standing-soba chains, with this Suidobashi branch being one of many locations across the city rather than an independent shop.

chef_bio.background: The shop's owner, Shida Akihisa (nicknamed "Dai-ō," meaning "the King," hence the shop's name), has a Taiwanese mother and spent time as a child in Taipei, particularly in the old downtown district of Wanhua near Longshan Temple — an area he describes as feeling like Taipei's own Asakusa. He grew up eating douhua there and, after years of self-taught trial and error trying to recreate the authentic texture and flavor he remembered, opened Asakusa's first dedicated douhua specialty shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: Shida's stated goal is to spread douhua in Japan in a form that suits Japanese palates, treating himself as something of a "missionary" for the dessert. Beyond the shop, he runs douhua-making classes for individuals and groups, and several of his students have gone on to open their own douhua-related shops elsewhere in Japan.

The shop also serves Taiwanese-style shaved ice and the street snack congyoubing (scallion pancake).

anecdotes.text: The shop's name comes from the crisp 'chaccha' sound the melted back fat makes as it is strained through a sieve and ladled over the ramen at the finish.

chef_bio.origin: California, USA (Culver City, 1958); first Japan location, 1991
chef_bio.background: Sizzler began in 1958 when the Johnson family opened a steakhouse in Culver City, California, paring the menu down to two cuts of steak with salad and bread and serving it through a then-novel self-service format so a steak dinner could be affordable. The brand landed in Japan in 1991, and this Shinjuku Mitsui Building restaurant was Japan's very first Sizzler. The store closed in December 2023 for a full renovation and reopened in May 2025 with a 'catering party'-inspired layout built around a slimmer, easier-to-navigate salad bar.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built on Sizzler's founding idea of making a steak dinner accessible through a self-serve, all-you-can-eat format centered on a big salad bar rather than a formal steakhouse experience.
chef_bio.specialty: Premium Salad Bar with 70+ rotating items — fresh vegetables, deli salads, soups, pasta, tacos and desserts — served alongside grilled steaks; the all-you-can-eat Cheese Toast is a house classic dating back to the original 1968 Sizzler Hollywood menu.

anecdotes.text: Sizzler's Cheese Toast first appeared in 1968 at the original Sizzler in Hollywood and has been served all-you-can-eat, just like the salad bar, at Sizzler locations worldwide ever since, including here.

This location was Sizzler's first restaurant in Japan when it opened in 1991; after an 18-month renovation the flagship reopened in May 2025 and the brand ran a year-long 'ALL-STAR REVIVAL FAIR' revisiting menu items from its 34 years in Japan.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The self-serve Premium Salad Bar places wheat-containing items — bread, pasta, and taco tortillas — on the same buffet line as the fresh vegetables and fruit, using shared serving utensils, so cross-contact is likely for anyone strictly avoiding gluten.

Sizzler is a chain which typically means a high risk of cross-contact, and it is likely not possible to dine safely at this establishment if you have celiac disease or must avoid cross-contact; the Shinjuku Mitsui location is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease.

The Premium Salad Bar offers 70+ items always available including seasonal vegetables, fresh deli salads, soup, fruit, pasta, tacos, dessert and drinks — all set out on the same self-serve bar, i.e., wheat items (pasta, tacos/tortillas, bread) physically alongside produce.

EU/US 'gluten-free labeling' and Japan's 'allergy labeling' are based on different standards; gluten-free does not necessarily mean wheat-free — Japan has no unified gluten-free standard, so an allergen menu does not equal celiac-safe handling.

Salad bar dressings are numerous (5 dressings, 6 vinegars, 3 oils, plus mayonnaise) and not itemized for allergens at the bar; Japanese buffet soups/dressings commonly rely on bonito dashi and contain dairy/egg — relevant to hidden animal products for vegans and unlabeled gluten sources.

positives.text: With 70+ items including whole fresh seasonal vegetables and fruit, the salad bar gives diners plenty of naturally plant-based, unprocessed options to build a meal around without relying on prepared or sauced dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A Japanese-run American-concept chain restaurant with a visual, point-and-serve salad bar that's easy to navigate with minimal Japanese, though menus and staff are not confirmed to be English-fluent at this specific location.

chef_bio.background: Butayama is part of Gift Holdings, the Tokyo ramen company built by Sho Tagawa, who trained at the noted Yokohama-style shop Ichirokuya before founding the Iekei chain Machida Shoten in 2008. Butayama grew out of Tagawa's personal love of Jiro-style ramen: its first shop opened in Machida in July 2018, at a time when chain-expanding the notoriously idiosyncratic Jiro genre was almost unheard of. It has since grown into Japan's largest Jiro-inspired chain, with roughly 50 locations across nine prefectures; the Shibuya Sakura Stage shop opened December 24, 2025, as the brand's first location right by Shibuya Station.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built to make intimidating Jiro-style ramen approachable for people who find the genre's original shops hard to navigate, especially women, families, and first-timers, through printed ordering guides at every table, a smaller portion option, and attentive service, without diluting the genre's hallmark volume and richness. The parent company's stated motto is 'ramen, as a gift to the world. '
chef_bio.specialty: Jiro-style ramen with thick, chewy all-wheat noodles, a semi-emulsified pork-bone and soy broth, tender braised pork, and a tall pile of cabbage and bean sprouts, customizable with garlic, extra vegetables, and oil ('mashimashi' add-ons); a smaller 125g noodle portion is also offered.

anecdotes.text: Butayama's first shop opened in Machida in July 2018 — at the time, chain-expanding a Jiro-inspired ramen concept was almost unprecedented. It has since grown into Japan's largest Jiro-style chain.

The chain was founded by Sho Tagawa, who trained at the Yokohama-style ramen shop Ichirokuya before opening the Iekei chain Machida Shoten in 2008; Butayama grew out of his personal enthusiasm for Jiro-style ramen.

Every table carries a printed guide to the Jiro-style ordering calls, a mini 125g noodle size is offered for smaller appetites, and staff provide paper aprons; the brand states on its official social media that it 'aims to be a shop that's easy for women and families with children to enter.'
The parent company's stated motto is 'ramen, as a gift to the world.'

cultural_comfort.note: The brand prints simplified ordering-call instructions at every table specifically to help newcomers and women navigate the intimidating Jiro-style ordering ritual, but there is no confirmed English menu, so some Japanese comprehension or willingness to point at the printed guide is still needed.

Matcha used across the brand is chosen by tea connoisseur Haruhide Morita, and the shop emphasizes serving koicha (thick tea) grade matcha rather than the usucha typically used in matcha desserts.

positives.text: The house soba (including the signature matcha soba) is made in-house daily as 十割そば — 100% buckwheat flour with no wheat flour used as a binder in the noodle itself.
